newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - S.African rate prospects - By E. Osborn.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - S.African rate prospects - By E. Osborn.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd
The high season of speculation about changes to Bank rate in the year ahead is upon us again.
In recent years, in the early months, the mood has swung from strong optimism to quiet resignation.

Initially there is optimism for cuts of two or three percentage steps dependent on the natural ebullience of the soothsayer, but essentially based on normative notions of what ought to happen in view of patently too high real interest rate structures.
The resignation sets in as there is growing understanding of the problems that the Governor has to wrestle with and the parameters that he has established for the execution of monetary policy.

Central bankers the world over are men of principle enjoined with the special task of combating inflation. There has to be a basic theory underlying their deliberations and that is the one of monetarism, which links inflation, or the loss of money values, to the supply of money.

It matters not whether there is truly such a definitive link, whether the association is causal or accommodative, and what time lags are involved. Much empirical research has gone into these things without coming to a definitive conclusion.

The real fact is that central bankers have to be guided by some set of principles and they have opted for the monetarist principles as intuitively correct. Thereafter the art of central banking lies in the judgements made about the course of financial, monetary and economic developments on the basis of indifferent lagged statistics or banking aggregates that are firm but difficult to interpret.

One of the rituals of the economic calendar in South Africa is the announcement of the monetary targets by the Governor. Such targets have mostly gone out of fashion elsewhere in the world, but for the notable exception of the arch protagonist of monetarism, the Bundesbank, Germany's central bank.

The Governor declared the M3 guidelines for 1997 as six percent to ten percent, unchanged on those for 1996. They reflect the Reserve Bank's resolve to bring the money supply growth down to a level compatible with lower inflation.

According to the Governor, the upper limit of ten percent takes account of a possible growth in real GDP of between two percent and three percent and the lower limit of six percent reflects the Bank's determination to reduce the rate of inflation over the longer term to levels more in line with that of South Africa's main trading partners and competitors.

These targets are meaningless when they are not even remotely likely to be achieved. Furthermore they are otiose in that the functions and responsibilities of the Governor in terms of eliminating inflation are universally known. However, they may serve as signpost and reminder of the obvious.
But more pertinently, they serve as a shield for the Governor when he appears obdurate in the face of apparently favourable developments, but not sufficient for his taste or confidence.

Incidentally there is a small but assertive local school with an "idee fixe" that the Reserve Bank should influence the money supply through manipulation of the so-called M0 aggregate of notes and coin instead of influencing the money supply indirectly through Bank rate.

Somehow it escapes the understanding of this school that the Bank has no power of influencing M0. Issued notes and coin are autonomously as demanded by the public. Whether the broad aggregate of money supply is really sensitive to the Bank rate in any tangible time span is another issue, but nevertheless it remains as fundamental to the tenets of central banking.

Central bankers take it is as given that changes to the interest rate structure, as caused by movements of Bank rate, influence the demand for bank credit. This in turn must affect the money supply because credit creation is the primal generator of new money. The final outcome for M3, however, is subject to the net effects of shifts in balances with the outside world and with the central government sector.

The association of M3 change and credit creation is strongly confirmed by the monthly analysis of M3 changes are reported in the Bank's monthly Selected Statistics. Over the last year credit creation with the private sector has amounted to 49 billion rand and M3 has grown by 38 billion rand, with the major cause of the lower M3 growth figure being the drain on the balance of payments.

Ironically, since the last increase in Bank rate last November, there has been a persistent substantial monthly increase in private sector credit, averaging 1.6 percent per month. The major thrust has come from other loans and advances, which is largely business credit in the first instance as opposed to household credit, in the first instance in that some credit to businesses advancing consumer credit in its various forms.

The recent monthly increases have averaged 2.7 percent. By comparison the average monthly increase on mortgage advances has been fractionally greater than one percent. Some of the mortgage business could be with businesses. Overall an inspection of the recent strong surge in credit demand confirms the Reserve Bank's own conclusion that the credit demand has been business driven.

Whether this is in respect of inventory financing or distress financing or normal bank financing of an economic surge is impossible to say. There is, however, little evidence in the figures, especially the bill finance figures, that the surge in credit demands is due to a shift in foreign trade finance from offshore to onshore.

There has been a particularly strong surge in manufacturing activity in the first quarter, as evidenced in the reported manufacturing indices, seasonally adjusted. From an average of 103.0 (base 1990) in the final quarter of 1996 the average for the first two months of 1997 was 108.1. Admittedly this was largely concentrated in the chemicals and non-ferrous basic metals industries, but there was evidence of an improvement over a broad front in the rest of manufacturing.

Now the upshot of all this is that the evidence is coming through fairly strongly that 1997 is to be a year of firm economic growth, and indeed even more so than in 1996, when a poor performance in the economy was accompanied by a strong agricultural performance. In 1997 agriculture will slip back but the non-agricultural economy will be much improved. There is a shadow over mining, however, while the rand remains stable. A reverse ebbing of foreign portfolio investments would weaken the rand and bring relief again to the mining industry - but strengthen the Governor's resolve to hold up interest rates.

The overall prospects are, therefore, for a continuation of business-oriented credit demand and, hence, the continued growth of M3. And this could continue right through 1997, in which case there will be no relaxation of monetary policy, or reduction in Bank rate, in the year.

There is general consensus that CPI inflation will continue rising for a few months and then slip back somewhat. However, the extent of any improvement is unlikely to be sufficient to impress the Governor, who will still be facing strong growth in M3 figures.
In conclusion it would appear unlikely that there will be any movement of Bank rate in 1997.

However, if there is a slump in economic growth for any reason and a consequential slow-down of M3 growth, a modest one percentage movement at best could happen. There is, therefore, but a remote chance of a one percentage point drop in Bank rate in the fourth quarter.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
